sm: Keith Foskey opens this episode of a Bow Tie Dialogue, where he hosts someone with a different theological view. His guest is Pastor Michael Grant of the Testing the Spirits podcast, and the topic is dispensationalism, the resurrection and the end times. Keith thanks Michael for being willing to talk after an earlier disagreement online. They discuss whether their channels count as discernment ministry. Michael says he dislikes that label because all Christians should be discerning, and he sees his work as apologetics, defending the faith.

Michael continues on apologetics and says the term heresy hunter makes little sense because false teachers are everywhere, and he thinks every pastor should address them. He says he started his channel in 2019 to upload shortened sermons for a radio station, and it grew after a local cult needed addressing. Keith says his own show started in 2020. Keith then explains the earlier disagreement. As an amillennialist he sees one general resurrection, which he also calls the rapture, followed by judgment. He asks Michael for his background, and Michael says he grew up in a dispensational church near Northfield, Massachusetts.

Michael notes that Northfield was a hub of dispensationalism, with C. I. Scofield and D. L. Moody there. He does not like the label and calls himself a leaky dispensationalist in the John MacArthur vein. Listening to R. C. Sproul led him to retest his beliefs, and he rejects Scofield's split between the kingdom of God and kingdom of heaven. He holds that the rapture and the resurrection are the same event in First Thessalonians 4, with further resurrections for people who die during the millennium. Keith says he holds progressive covenantalism, the Kingdom through Covenant view, and sees Michael as close to progressive dispensationalists.

Keith describes progressive covenantalism and progressive dispensationalism as attempts to bridge the two camps, and says he sees the millennium as the present age between Christ's comings. Michael says he differs from historic premillennialism because of the pre-tribulation rapture and the distinction between church and Israel. He says he has never read John Nelson Darby, that Darby did not invent the rapture, and that he finds some original Scofield notes problematic. He has never met a mid-Acts dispensationalist, though Keith has. Michael says he cannot accept that this age is the millennium, and Keith asks what the millennium is for.

Michael says Christians still pray thy kingdom come, and that Satan is not bound now, since Peter described him as a roaring lion. He lays out his sequence: worsening times, a seven-year tribulation under the antichrist, then Christ's return to the Mount of Olives and a literal thousand-year reign from Jerusalem. He says that if amillennialism were true he would stop teaching the Bible. He says the millennium fulfils the promises to Abraham and Israel. Those who survive the tribulation populate it, alongside the saints in glorified bodies, which he compares to Jesus's forty days on earth after rising.

Michael says the millennium will not be perfect, since Christ rules with a rod of iron and Satan leads one last rebellion at its end. Keith asks whether there are still nations and whether the earth is still plagued by disasters. Michael guesses there will be nations on a radically changed earth, and says the millennium is a prelude to the new heaven and new earth. They discuss Doug Wilson and older postmillennialism, and Keith says Wilson's view resembles optimistic amillennialism. Michael asks if amillennialism is really a form of postmillennialism, since Christ returns after the millennium in both.

Keith agrees that amillennialism and postmillennialism are both postmillennial, differing on when the millennium begins. Michael argues that although comforts and science improve, spiritually things are getting worse, and he says we are in the great falling away. Keith agrees things are bad but says the medieval church was bad too, with popes put on trial after death and reformers burned at the stake. Michael replies that Rome's teachings are worse today, citing blessings of same-sex unions and universalism.

Michael says modern church leaders are more spiritually depraved even if medieval ones could do worse things. Keith adds that Rome is a different church after Vatican Two, and Michael sees it moving toward a one-world religion. Keith says he also expects apostasy, tribulation and a final antichrist system, but does not require a pre-tribulation rapture or an intermediate kingdom. They discuss whether Jew and Gentile distinctions last into eternity. Keith says all Israel's promises are fulfilled in Christ and we are grafted in through union with him. He says this is neither supersessionism nor classic covenant theology.

Keith explains that Christ recapitulated Israel's history, going through Egypt, the waters and the wilderness, and so is the true Israel and the singular seed. Michael points to Romans 11 and a future for Israel. Keith agrees with Sproul that a revival among ethnic Jews is likely, but objects to equating the modern state with the Israel of God. Michael rejects John Hagee's view that Jews have their own covenant. Michael raises Jeremiah 31, saying Israel will never cease being a nation. Keith says that means a people united to Christ, and that the land promise is the whole new creation.

Michael agrees that all the promises are fulfilled in Christ, but says some are still unfulfilled and they differ on when and how. Keith says he prays for Jewish people to come to Christ and rejects the idea that they are saved apart from faith, citing a Pat Robertson remark. Michael says this issue should not divide Christians, though hardcore replacement theology and antisemitism are a problem. Michael thanks Keith, is happy to return, and says his channel is Pastor Michael Grant, the podcast is Testing the Spirits, and his church is Morris Corner Church in Western Massachusetts. Keith closes the show.
